subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: First Read — The Lagori Champions (Part I)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 73–79): shared read-aloud of dialogue-narrative Part I with new vocabulary.

time_bands.activity: Let us Read (pp. 73–79): introduce the setting — Sundarpur village, Ravi, and his cousin Prakash from Rajasthan. Ask students what games they play outdoors before opening the text.
Let us Read (pp. 73–79): teacher reads Part I aloud expressively, tracking characters — Guneet, Deepa, Nidhi, Imran — and pausing at dialogue. Students follow in their textbooks.

Let us Read (pp. 73–79): revisit new words — match, stacked, opponent, boundary, referee, dodged, teamwork, warriors, cousin — using context from the just-read passage. Students repeat each word in the sentence it appeared.
Let us Read (pp. 73–79): quick whole-class oral check — ask two or three students to say in their own words what Prakash learns about Lagori from Imran. Accept oral responses only.

periods.teacher_notes: Students meet a new setting and several named characters at once; pause after each character's introduction so the class can keep track of who is who. The discovery that Lagori and Satoliya are the same game is a key moment — let students react to it naturally before moving on. Unanchored comprehension questions from the Let us Think sections remain available for self-reading alongside the textbook.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading — Part I Comprehension Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p. 76): four short-answer questions on Part I events and game details.
Let us Think A (p. 80): five questions — game rules, team name, Prakash's selection, and villagers' celebration.

time_bands.activity: Brief re-read of the passage section where Imran explains the rules and Prakash names the game Satoliya (pp. 75–77). Students follow along as the teacher reads two key paragraphs aloud.

Let us Think (p. 76): teacher poses each of the four questions — who joined the group, how many stones and what kind, which state calls it Satoliya, and the opponent team's name. Students answer orally in pairs, then one pair shares per question for class confirmation.

Let us Think A (p. 80): work through all five questions together — what Lagori is and how it is played, the team name and opponents, why Prakash was selected, who explained the rules, and what the villagers did after the Tigers won. Students write brief answers in their notebooks.
Teacher invites two students to share one written answer each and offers brief feedback on sentence completeness and relevant detail.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who are unsure about game rules may blend story details with outside knowledge — anchor every answer back to what the text says explicitly, particularly Imran's explanation. Having discussed Lagori's rules and regional names in the first read helps students answer the Part I questions with confidence here.

periods.activity_title: Read Part II — Match Day Drama and Consolidation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p. 79): four questions on Part II — whistle, first shot, Prakash's final act, handshake.
Let us Think C (p. 81): five true/false statements on story facts.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think D (p. 81): fill in three blanks about Ravi's appearance, the captain's name, and joys the match reminded everyone of.

time_bands.activity: Let us Read (pp. 77–79): shared reading of Part II — teacher and students alternate paragraphs, tracking how the match unfolds from Deepa's first hit to Prakash's winning seventh stone.

Let us Think (p. 79): four short-answer questions — who blew the whistle, who took the first shot, what Prakash did before the final whistle, and why both teams shook hands. Students respond in writing, then compare with a partner.
Let us Think C (p. 81): teacher reads each true/false statement aloud. Students write T or F and one brief reason from the text. Class discusses answers together.
Whole-class discussion: Deepa says Lagori is more exciting than video games. Ask students to share a word or short phrase from the story that supports her view. Accept oral responses only.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse Nidhi taking the first shot with Deepa scoring it — the passage distinguishes between different moments, so direct students to re-read the relevant line. The fill-in exercise on page 81 (Let us Think D) works well as reinforcement at home, where students can locate the answers at their own pace.

periods.activity_title: Sequencing and Story Mapping — Events in Order

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think E (p. 81): number seven sentences in the order events occur in the story.

time_bands.activity: Recap the main story arc by asking students to call out five key moments from the match — whistle, first shot, rebuild, seventh stone, handshake — and write them on the board in whatever order students suggest.

Let us Think E (p. 81): distribute the seven sentences (teacher writes them on the board or reads aloud one by one). Students number them in the correct story order individually in their notebooks. They then compare with a neighbour and resolve any differences by pointing to the text.

Whole-class sequence check: teacher calls on different students for each numbered position, building the correct order on the board. Discuss one or two disagreements — which clue in the story settled the order?
Students retell the match in three spoken sentences using the agreed sequence. One or two volunteers share; the class gives a thumbs-up if the order matches the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Sequencing tasks reveal whether students hold the story as a connected whole or as isolated facts — watch for students who anchor correctly on Prakash's seventh stone but misplace the handshake scene. Having read both parts of the story, students now hold enough detail to justify each order choice by pointing to the text.

periods.activity_title: Discussion and Listening — Teamwork, Traditions, and Odd-One-Out

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 80): three guided discussion prompts — clapping for both teams, teamwork, and Lagori vs. video games.
Let us Listen (p. 84): teacher reads five sentences aloud; students identify the word that does not belong.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B (p. 80): pose each of the three discussion questions in turn — why both captains' hands were raised, how teamwork helps a team win, and whether Lagori is more exciting than video games. Students share views in pairs for a brief moment then contribute to whole-class discussion; teacher builds on responses.

Let us Listen (p. 84): teacher reads each of the five sentences clearly at a natural pace and repeats once. Students listen for the word that does not belong to the sports/games category in each sentence.

Let us Listen (p. 84): teacher reads all five sentences a final time. Students write the odd-one-out word for each sentence, then share answers aloud sentence by sentence. Teacher confirms with a brief explanation of why the word is out of category.

Let us Speak B (p. 85): each student thinks of one community game or match from their own village or neighbourhood and tells a partner about it in two sentences. Two or three pairs share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The Let us Think B discussion on clapping for both teams and lifting both captains' hands connects directly to the sportsmanship theme woven through the story's closing scene. For the listening task, students at this stage sometimes write before the sentence ends — encourage them to listen to the full sentence before identifying the odd word.

periods.activity_title: Find a Classmate — Guided Conversation Game

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (pp. 84–85): walk-around activity — find classmates who match twenty given descriptions.

time_bands.activity: Let us Speak A (pp. 84–85): teacher models the activity — demonstrate asking a student 'Do you enjoy outdoor games?' and recording the name. Explain that students must form a complete question and listen for the answer before writing.

Let us Speak A (pp. 84–85): students circulate, asking each other the twenty questions from the list — favourites, habits, and experiences such as who loves Lagori or Satoliya, who has visited a sports stadium, and who has a bat or ball. Each student keeps a record in their notebook.

Class reconvenes. Teacher calls out selected items from the list and asks: 'How many of you found someone who…?' Students raise hands and share the name they found. Celebrate any classmate who matches multiple items.
Brief debrief: what was the most surprising thing a classmate told you? Two or three students share in one sentence each.

periods.teacher_notes: The guided-conversation format reinforces complete-sentence questioning — prompt students who use single words ('stadium?') to rephrase as a full question. The Lagori or Satoliya item is likely to prompt a rich exchange given the story's celebration of the game across regions.

periods.activity_title: Words and Their Meanings — Synonyms and Antonyms, Unscrambling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (pp. 82–83): circle the word that does NOT share meaning — eight synonym-antonym sets.
Let us Learn B (p. 83): unscramble four letter-sets using meaning hints.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn A (pp. 82–83): teacher writes the first set — 'large / huge / tiny / big' — on the board and asks students to explain how they would decide which word does not belong. Draw out the concept of synonym vs. word that means the opposite or something different.
Let us Learn A (pp. 82–83): students work through all eight sets in their textbooks, circling the odd word out. Teacher circulates, asking students to justify one choice aloud before marking it.

Let us Learn B (p. 83): teacher reads each hint aloud — 'a place or region beyond a boundary', 'to raise your hand and wave it in greeting', 'a sports event between two teams', 'a child of your aunt or uncle' — and students arrange the scrambled letters to find each word. They write the answer and then use the word in a spoken sentence.
Class check for both tasks: students call out answers one set at a time. For any disagreement, return briefly to the meaning hint or the sentence context from the story to confirm.

periods.teacher_notes: In Let us Learn A, students sometimes choose 'activity' as the odd word for 'contest' when 'playground' is the correct answer — encourage students to test each word in the original sentence before deciding. The unscrambling in Let us Learn B works best when students say the hint aloud first and think of the word before touching the letters.

periods.activity_title: Word Hunt, Sentence Rearrangement, and Sentence vs. Question

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p. 86): rearrange five scrambled word groups into correct sentences.
Let us Write C (p. 87): tick whether each of five given lines is a sentence or a question.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 85): find at least six story words in the word-search grid and use each in a sentence.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write B (p. 86): teacher writes the first scrambled group on the board — 'boundary / field / is / the / marked / a / with' — and invites students to arrange the words. Discuss what makes the rearranged version a correct English sentence (subject, verb, clear meaning).

Let us Write B (p. 86): students work through the remaining four scrambled groups individually in their notebooks — Prakash looking with surprise, a dancing peacock, clouds in the sky, plants needing water. Teacher circulates and prompts where students are stuck.

Let us Write C (p. 87): teacher reads each of the five items aloud. Students tick 'Sentence' or 'Question' in their textbooks. Class compares answers; teacher asks: 'How did you know this one was a question?' to elicit clues such as question words and rising punctuation.
Students write one sentence and one question of their own about the Lagori match — anything from the story. Two or three volunteers share; class decides whether each is correctly labelled.

periods.teacher_notes: Sentence rearrangement reveals whether students have internalised subject-verb order — common errors include placing the verb before the subject or anchoring on a content word rather than the grammatical frame. The word-search and sentence-writing task sent home works best when students re-read their textbook passage to spot familiar words in the grid.

periods.activity_title: Lagori Team Badge Design and Spot-the-Difference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do A (p. 87): design a Lagori team badge in groups, choose a name, and present to class.
Let us Do B (p. 88): find and point out eight differences between two Lagori game pictures.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do A (p. 87): divide the class into groups of four or five. Each group chooses a team name — teacher gives two examples from the task, such as Rainbow Runners or Sky Warriors — and decides two or three values or symbols their badge will show.

Let us Do A (p. 87): groups design their Lagori team badge on a drawing sheet using coloured pencils, markers, and any decorative materials available. The badge must include the team name and at least one element that connects to Lagori or teamwork — stacked stones, a ball, or a symbol of unity.

Let us Do A (p. 87): each group holds up their badge and one speaker explains the team name and one design choice — what it represents and how it reflects the spirit of Lagori. Class listens and may ask one brief question per group.

Let us Do B (p. 88): students open their textbooks to the two pictures. Working individually, they spot and point out the eight differences, circling them in pencil. Two or three students share their list of differences with the class to confirm.

periods.teacher_notes: Groups sometimes spend most of the badge-making time debating the team name — suggest they agree on the name within the first two minutes and move quickly to the design. The spot-the-difference activity on page 88 sharpens careful visual observation; encourage students to be systematic (top to bottom, left to right) rather than random in their search.

items.item_stem: Read the sentences below and mark each one True or False. Write one word from the story to support your answer for any one statement you mark False.

options.text: Deepa placed the winning seventh stone before the final whistle.
Imran explained the rules of Lagori to Prakash.
Prakash had played Lagori many times before visiting Sundarpur.
The Sundarpur Tigers played against a team called the Green Warriors.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is False — Prakash had never heard of Lagori before Imran explained it. Statement 4 is False — Prakash (not Deepa) placed the winning seventh stone just before the final whistle.

items.item_stem: Put the events from the Lagori match in the order they happen in the story. Write the numbers 1 to 4 next to the events below.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Event | Order |
|---|---|
| The referee blew the whistle to start the match. | |
| Prakash placed the seventh stone just before the final whistle. | |
| The two teams shook hands and appreciated each other. | |
| Deepa's team began rebuilding the stack of stones. | |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 – The referee blew the whistle; 2 – Deepa's team began rebuilding; 3 – Prakash placed the seventh stone; 4 – The two teams shook hands.

answer_key.left: The referee blew the whistle to start the match.
Deepa's team began rebuilding the stack of stones.
Prakash placed the seventh stone just before the final whistle.
The two teams shook hands and appreciated each other.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the sentence below aloud twice. Listen carefully and choose the word that does NOT belong with the others in the list. My brother likes to play Kabbadi, basketball, badminton, kho-kho, knitting and Lagori.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this may not yet distinguish games from crafts, grouping ball-sports separately.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing kho-kho suggests the student focused on unfamiliarity with the game name rather than its category.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing Lagori suggests the student connected the word to the story and overlooked that it is also a game.

items.item_stem: At the end of the Lagori match, the referee lifted the hands of both captains and the crowd cheered for both teams — even though only one team won. Do you think this was fair? Tell your teacher in two or three sentences, giving one reason from the story and one from your own thinking.

expected_elements: States a clear yes or no opinion.
Gives one reason from the story's ending.
Connects to fairness or sportsmanship in own words.

items.item_stem: Look at the words below and tick the correct box to show whether it forms a sentence or a question when read as written.

options.text: Deepa is the captain of the Sundarpur Tigers. — This is a sentence.
Did Prakash place the last stone? — This is a sentence.
The villagers celebrated the Tigers' victory. — This is a question.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is True — it is a complete sentence ending with a full stop and making a statement. Statement 2 is False — it is a question beginning with 'Did' and ending with a question mark. Statement 3 is False — it is a sentence, not a question, because it states a fact and ends with a full stop.

expected_elements: All seven words used in the sentence.
Sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

items.item_stem: Three words are given for the word in bold. Choose the one word that does NOT mean the same as the bold word.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose 'rebuild' may not recognise that rebuilding is a form of repairing.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Students who choose 'mend' may be guessing rather than thinking about meaning.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose 'fix' have likely not checked that 'fix' and 'repair' share the same meaning.

| Badge Design Element | Story Idea It Represents |
|---|---|
| Seven stacked stones | The goal of the Lagori game |
| Two hands joined together | Sportsmanship and shaking hands after the match |
| A running figure | Prakash being chosen because he is a fast runner |
| A tiger | The Sundarpur Tigers team name |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Seven stacked stones → The goal of the Lagori game; Two hands joined → Sportsmanship and shaking hands; A running figure → Prakash chosen for being a fast runner; A tiger → The Sundarpur Tigers team name.
